q: A metal capsule on a French bottle carries an image of Marianne and a departmental number in place of the producer's own design. What is it?
opts: A duty-paid capsule that also serves as the movement document
A mark showing the wine was bottled by a co-operative cellar
A guarantee the bottle has not been opened and refilled
A seal applied by the appellation authority after tasting
exp: The capsule-conge is bought from the French revenue and shows the duty settled, which lets the bottle travel without separate accompanying paperwork. Colour separates the fiscal families, wine from vin doux naturel from spirits, though it no longer separates an appellation wine from an IGP, since a single lie-de-vin capsule has been allowed to stand for either since 2011. The number identifies the department where the bottler is registered.

q: A numbered paper strip crosses the neck of an Italian bottle and tears when the capsule is cut. What does it show?
opts: A numbered seal issued by the state for a denominated wine
That the producer belongs to a growers' consortium
That the wine has been aged the minimum period for its category
That the bottle was filled at the estate rather than by a merchant
exp: The strip comes from the state printer and is issued in a controlled quantity to each producer, so the number of bottles claimed for a denomination can be checked against the seals handed out. It is a policing device and carries no verdict on how good the wine is.

q: The vintage is printed on a narrow band around the neck and nowhere on the main label. What does that arrangement buy the producer?
opts: The wine escapes the rules governing vintage statements
One main label serves every year
The bottle can be sold in markets that forbid a vintage
The year can be altered after the wine has been released, since the band is not the label
exp: Main labels are printed in long runs and neck bands in short ones, so splitting the year off is simply cheaper. It also means the year can go missing: soak a neck band off in an ice bucket and the bottle no longer says what it is.

q: Drawing the cork from an old bottle reveals an estate name and a year branded along its side. What does that add to what the label says?
opts: Proof that the wine has never been recorked or topped up since it left the cellar where it was filled
A guarantee that the wine inside is still in good condition
Evidence that the bottle was filled by hand
Corroboration of the estate and the vintage claimed
exp: A branded cork is a second and independent statement of the same facts, and a mismatch between cork and label is among the oldest warnings of an invented bottle. It settles nothing about the condition of the wine, which only the glass can tell you.

q: Raised letters and numbers are moulded into the base and lower body of the glass, where no label reaches. What do they identify?
opts: The vintage of the wine inside
The glassworks and the mould
The alcoholic strength of the wine
The number of bottles the producer filled during that particular bottling run
exp: Bottle makers mark their moulds so a faulty batch can be traced back to the plant that made it, much as a lot code traces a fill. Many moulds carry the year the bottle itself was made as well. The marks belong to the glass rather than to the wine, and glass dated later than the vintage is a well-known sign of a fake.

q: A guest wants to buy tonight's wine again at home and asks you to write it down. Which three elements must you copy?
opts: Producer, appellation and vintage
Brand name, colour and price
Importer, alcohol and volume
Bar code and size
exp: Those three narrow a wine to one product from one year, which is what any merchant needs in order to search for it. Artwork and fanciful names are redesigned and reused constantly, and a guest who remembers only the picture on the front is very hard to help.

q: The label is mould-stained and cockled and has lifted at one corner, while the fill sits high in the neck. What does the paper's condition suggest?
opts: Long storage somewhere cool and damp
That the bottle has been refilled and relabelled
That wine has leaked past the cork at some point and dried across the glass and the paper
That the bottle stood upright in a warm room
exp: Damp cellars ruin paper and look after corks, so a battered label above a good fill is usually reassuring rather than alarming. It is the level of the wine in the neck rather than the state of the printing that is worth watching.

q: A regular guest insists a bottle is not the wine they had last month because the label looks entirely different, though every regulated statement on the glass is unchanged. What has happened?
opts: The bottle comes from a different market and holds a different blend
The wine has been relabelled after a reclassification
The wine has been rebottled by another company
The producer has redesigned the label
exp: Artwork is changed for commercial reasons and carries no legal information whatever, which makes it the least reliable way to recognise a wine. Read the regulated statements instead, since those are the lines a producer cannot restyle at will, and the guest can be reassured on the spot.

q: Travelling inland from the Atlantic, in what order do the four broad Loire wine regions appear?
opts: Anjou-Saumur, then Pays Nantais, then Touraine, then the Centre
Pays Nantais, then Anjou-Saumur, then Touraine, then the Centre
The Centre, then Touraine, then Anjou-Saumur, then Pays Nantais
Touraine, then the Centre, then Anjou-Saumur, then Pays Nantais
exp: The river meets the Atlantic at Saint-Nazaire, some fifty kilometres below Nantes, so the Pays Nantais is the seaward end and the Centre lies furthest upstream, roughly four hundred kilometres inland. Every soil, grape and climate change follows that line.

q: Vineyards near Nantes ripen in mild damp air off the ocean, while those around Sancerre face hard winters and a real frost risk. What is that eastward shift?
opts: A uniform maritime climate along the whole valley
Mediterranean influence giving way to an alpine climate
Maritime influence giving way to a continental climate
Continental influence giving way to a maritime climate
exp: The Atlantic reaches only so far inland. Losing its moderating effect means colder winters, warmer summers and sharper vintage variation at the eastern end of the valley.

q: Two entirely different bedrocks meet in the middle of the valley: ancient schist and granite to the west, soft chalky limestone to the east. What are those geological domains called?
opts: The Jura arc and the volcanic Aquitaine Basin
The Massif Central and the Rhone graben
The Vosges massif and the Rhine rift valley
The Massif Armoricain and the Paris Basin
exp: The join runs near Saumur. West of it the rock is hard, acidic and hundreds of millions of years old; east of it lies the sedimentary limestone that also underlies Paris.

q: One Loire appellation group takes its name from a river of the basin spelled without the final e, north of Tours. Which appellation belongs to it?
opts: Bonnezeaux
Quincy
Jasnieres
Cheverny
exp: The Loir is a separate river from the Loire, and Jasnieres is its best-known appellation: a thin strip of south-facing tuffeau making severe, long-lived dry Chenin.

q: Wine grown along the valley but outside any district or village appellation is sold under which regional name?
opts: Vin de France
IGP Val de Loire
AOC Val de Loire
IGP Pays d'Oc
exp: The regional IGP covers the whole basin and is where varietal labelling and experimental plantings live. Vin de France carries no geographical claim at all, and Pays d'Oc belongs to the Languedoc.

q: A hard winter in 1709 killed most of the vineyard around Nantes, and growers replanted with a Burgundian white chosen for its hardiness. Which variety?
opts: Chenin Blanc
Aligote
Chardonnay
Melon de Bourgogne
exp: Melon survives cold better than what it replaced and ripens early enough for a damp Atlantic autumn. It has been the sole grape of Muscadet ever since, and is scarcely grown in Burgundy today.

q: Chardonnay's parents also produced the grape behind Muscadet. Which crossing is it?
opts: Traminer and Sauvignon Blanc
Chenin Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc
Pinot and Cabernet Franc
Pinot and Gouais Blanc
exp: The same humble Gouais Blanc crossed with Pinot gave Chardonnay, Aligote, Gamay and Melon among many others. Shared parentage says nothing about shared flavour, as these two demonstrate.

q: Winter is spent in tank without racking, and the wine goes into bottle straight off its fine sediment. Which label term records that?
opts: Elevage en fut de chene
Vieilles vignes
Vendange tardive
Sur lie
exp: The term is regulated rather than decorative: the wine must remain on its fine lees through the winter and be bottled directly off them in the year following the harvest.
